title: Quadratics by factorising
examples: Can you show me how to factorise this expression?
What do I do if the equation has no constant term?
Is it always best to factorise a quadratic equation?

explain.say: Today we are solving quadratic equations by factorising. Remember a quadratic equation has the form a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero. Our first step is to set the equation to zero.

items: Start with quadratic form: ax² + bx + c = 0

explain.say: We will use the zero product rule. This rule says if two things multiply to zero, then at least one of those things must be zero. This gives us two simpler equations to solve.

draw.text: If A times B = 0, then A = 0 or B = 0

explain.say: Let us look at the example x squared minus five x equals fourteen. First we must move the fourteen over to the left side. This makes the equation x squared minus five x minus fourteen equals zero.

Now we factorise the expression. We need two numbers that multiply to negative fourteen and add up to negative five. These numbers are negative seven and positive two. So we factorise it as (x minus seven) times (x plus two) equals zero.
Applying the zero product rule, we set each factor to zero. This gives us x minus seven equals zero, and also x plus two equals zero. Solving these gives us x equals seven and x equals negative two.

faq.q: What if the coefficient of x squared is not one?
faq.a: If the coefficient a is not one, you must factorise out the greatest common factor first. You might also need to use grouping methods. Another way to ask this is, what if a is not one? Or, how do I handle a different leading coefficient?
asks: What if a is not one?
How do I handle a different leading coefficient?

faq.q: Does the zero product rule always work for quadratics?
faq.a: Yes, the zero product rule is a fundamental property of multiplication. It applies whenever you have two or more factors multiplied together equaling zero. You can also ask, is the zero product rule always true? Or, does this rule work for all equations?
asks: Is the zero product rule always true?
Does this rule work for all equations?

faq.q: What if the equation does not have a number at the end?
faq.a: If there is no constant term, it means the last term is zero. You can factor out an x from every term in the equation. For example, x squared plus three x equals zero factors to x(x plus three) equals zero. You might ask, what if there is no constant term? Or, how do I start if the last term is zero?
asks: What if there is no constant term?
How do I start if the last term is zero?

faq.q: What do I do if I cannot factorise the quadratic?
faq.a: If you cannot factorise it easily, you should use a different method like the quadratic formula. The formula always works for any quadratic equation. You could ask, what if it doesn't factorise? Or, what is an alternative method?

faq.q: Is it necessary to factorise the equation first?
faq.a: Yes, for this method, setting the equation to zero and then factorising is the required first step. If you do not set it to zero, the zero product rule cannot be applied correctly. You might ask, must I set it to zero first? Or, is setting it to zero mandatory?
asks: Must I set it to zero first?
Is setting it to zero mandatory?

facts: A quadratic equation has the general form a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero.
The zero product rule states that if two factors multiply to zero, at least one factor must be zero.
To factorise, you look for two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.
When solving, you must set the entire equation equal to zero before factorising.

quiz.say: Solve x squared plus x equals 0
quiz.why: You factor out x, leaving x multiplied by (x plus one) equals zero. This gives two solutions, x equals zero and x equals negative one.

wrong.0: This is tempting because you might only consider the x squared term.
wrong.1: This is tempting because you might only solve for one factor.
wrong.3: This is tempting because you might incorrectly add the coefficients of x and the constant term.

wrong.0: This is tempting because you might only solve for the middle term.
wrong.2: This is tempting because you might incorrectly use the square root method.

quiz.say: If (x + 3)(x - 5) equals zero, what are the values of x?
quiz.why: Using the zero product rule, you set each factor to zero. Setting x plus three to zero gives x equals negative three, and setting x minus five to zero gives x equals five.

wrong.1: This is tempting because you might forget to change the sign when solving x plus three equals zero.
wrong.2: This is tempting because you might incorrectly add the numbers inside the brackets.
wrong.3: This is tempting because you might multiply the two numbers together instead of solving for each one.
